title: What Makes a Reply Actually Answer an Argument?
short: When a reply answers the argument
subtitle: A complete response-link audit and eight source-linked close readings.
finding: A useful reply changes the support for the claim actually being made—not merely a nearby claim.
statisticLabel: Of recorded reply-to-target links lead to another reply · 112 debates
explanation: The later-process assessments contain 2,444 replies and 2,978 links to the moves they address. Most links—1,733—lead to another reply, so following the exchange matters. All stored targets exist, and their excerpts start no later than the replies. These checks show that the recorded exchange can be followed; they do not establish that every reply succeeds.
detail: Eight worked examples show the difference between challenging a premise, exposing a missing inference, clarifying what was claimed, conceding a point, and answering a position the opponent did not state. Meyer distinguishes physical order from functional DNA sequences; Craig identifies a disputed inference from foreknowledge to necessity; Goff acknowledges a clarified objection. Each local success leaves a clearly identified question open. The paper also examines inaccurate attribution and incomplete responses.
limitation: The eight cases were deliberately selected to explain different reasoning moves, not to measure how often each side replies well. Existing scores are context, not independent confirmation of the analysis. The close readings use saved caption excerpts, not a new full-video review.

links.label: Donahue–Linford: counting options is not assigning probabilities

method: Extract all reply targets from the 112 later-process comparable ledgers and verify the ledger fingerprints, target existence and excerpt-start chronology. Count links separately from replies because one reply may address several moves. For eight deliberately selected cases, read the saved excerpts for the reply and its target, identify the step affected and state the remaining burden. This is an editorial framework, not a complete qualitative recoding of all 2,444 replies.

topic: From a cause to a religious claim
title: From a Creator to a Personal God: Which Steps Are Defended?
short: From a creator to a personal God
subtitle: Eight passages distinguish an ultimate source, agency, divine attributes and religious identification.
finding: An argument for a cause does not automatically establish a mind, perfect goodness or a particular religion.
statisticLabel: Six debates examining what supports each additional claim
explanation: The case studies separate a necessary foundation or cause from intelligence, purposes, unlimited attributes and religious identification. Several speakers explicitly defend the extra steps rather than simply assuming them. Craig offers an argument for personal agency; Jones argues for unlimited perfection and explores a route to the Trinity; Horn adds historical evidence for Christianity. Each proposed step has its own supporting reasons and unresolved questions.
detail: The paper also includes deliberate limits. Meyer distinguishes an inference from biological data from an argument based on scripture; even a successful biological-design argument would not alone establish a cosmic creator. Goff gives up unlimited divine power in response to suffering, which creates a new question about what limits that power. The practical rule applies to both sides: credit the conclusion actually supported, and do not treat a local criticism as a disproof of every possible creator.
limitation: These eight passages are a deliberately varied case study, not a census of creator arguments or a count of how often religious speakers overreach. The diagram distinguishes claims; it is not a compulsory sequence or a proof. Speaker identity and personal religion do not determine how an argument is classified.

Meyer–Atkins: a deliberately limited design claim

method: Read eight saved source passages selected to cover explicit additional inferences, disputed inferences and intentionally limited conclusions. Record the starting claim, proposed further conclusion, reason for the transition and remaining question. Include cosmology, biological design, divine attributes and historical identification across browsing categories. Use original scores only as context, not as a test of the new interpretation.

title: How Much Do Opponents Affect Recorded Performance?
subtitle: Repeated matchups and within-person comparisons do not support a dependable schedule correction.
finding: The small opponent-score association is not stable when the eligible comparison set changes.
statisticLabel: Fitted own-score change for a five-point higher opponent average · main and same-procedure checks
explanation: The study compares a person's own scores against opponents with different averages elsewhere, excluding every meeting of that pair from the opponent average. The main model uses 295 appearances and accounts for the speaker, assessment procedure and PRO/CON role. A five-point higher opponent average is associated with a 0.49-point lower own score. Requiring same-procedure opponent experience leaves 180 appearances and gives a 0.06-point increase. On those same 180 records, the original opponent measure already gives a near-zero 0.02-point decrease. The changed sample, not just the changed measure, matters.
detail: Among 21 pairs who meet more than once, only two switch which person scores higher; both comparisons cross assessment procedures. None of the 12 same-procedure repeat groups has a strict reversal. The typical range of margins is three points across all repeated pairs and two within the same procedure. This supports stability within those observed matchups, but not an automatic opponent-adjusted ranking. The paper shows eight model checks and distinguishes score changes from changes in the margin between speakers.
limitation: Opponents were not assigned at random. Their outside averages also reflect topics, schedules and judging conditions. The checks describe associations, not causal effects or advance predictions. The spread between models is not a confidence interval; the same-procedure check changes both the proxy and the eligible sample.

links.label: Related study: how stable are the rankings?
Explore the published rankings and sample sizes
Schieber–Rauser: one of the repeated pairs

method: Use all 291 comparable locked one-on-one debates for the pair inventory. For the fitted comparison, require at least three outside-pair appearances for the opponent and two eligible appearances for the focal speaker. Fit own score against the opponent's outside-pair average with separate speaker starting levels, then procedure and role adjustments. Check broad topics, equal-person weighting, five outside appearances, separate procedures and procedure-matched opponent averages. Hold the final check's 180 appearances fixed and restore the original pooled proxy to distinguish a sample change from a measure change. Independently reproduce all fits with a full design matrix.
